human_tolerance.notes: "Fox squirrels are tolerant of human proximity, and even thrive in crowded urban and suburban environments. They exploit human habitations for sources of food and nesting sites, being as happy nesting in an attic as they are in a hollow tree." Its habitat section names urban neighbourhoods with trees alongside forest patches as where it is most often found.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Females come into estrus in mid-December or early January, then again in June; high-pitched whines are given during mating.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Two litters a year, though yearling females may produce only one. Gestation runs 44-45 days; the earliest litters appear in late January and most births fall in mid-March and July.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Females become sexually mature at 10-11 months and usually first breed at a year old. Young are born blind and helpless, the eyes open at 4-5 weeks and the ears at 6; they are weaned at 12-14 weeks but may not be self-supporting until 16 weeks, and usually disperse in September or October, dening together or with their mother through their first winter.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Caches shelled, high-fat foods such as acorns and nuts by burying them for later.

vocalizations.description: A series of barks, the most common vocalization of the species, used to warn of approaching threats; loud distress screams carry that warning.
Clucking and chucking sounds, not unlike some game birds, which groups make together in spring and autumn; a small ruckus of several squirrels doing this is a common sight and sound.
Tooth chatters and breathy barks, given as indications of stress, and grunts and squeals from a restrained animal.
A high-pitched whine given during mating, around the mid-December and June estrus periods.

common_names.note: Wikipedia gives 'fox squirrel', also known as the eastern fox squirrel; the record uses the eastern form to separate it from Sciurus carolinensis, which also exists in this repository.

range.note: Most of the eastern United States, north into the southern prairie provinces of Canada, west to the Dakotas, Colorado and Texas, and south to northern Coahuila, Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas; absent except for vagrants from New England, New Jersey, most of New York, northern and eastern Pennsylvania, Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Introduced to California, Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Washington, New Mexico and Utah, and to Ontario and British Columbia. Since 2016 it has been on the EU list of Invasive Alien Species of Union concern, so invasive_in carries EU as a single code for that list rather than inventing member-state entries the source does not give.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: "Fox squirrels are strictly diurnal, non-territorial, and spend more of their time on the ground than most other tree squirrels. They are still, however, agile climbers."

traits.nest_type.note: Tree dens in natural or woodpecker-made cavities are preferred over leaf nests for winter and for raising young, so Cavity is the primary nest type and the summer drey is carried as a nest_platform resource.

traits.perching.note: Climbs and caches in trees but does not perch on a branch the way a bird does; set to false, matching the treatment of sciurus-carolinensis.

traits.senses.note: "Fox squirrels have excellent vision and well-developed senses of hearing and smell. They use scent-marking to communicate with other fox squirrels", and they carry vibrissae as touch receptors above and below the eyes, on the chin and nose and on each forearm - which is what vibration records here.

traits.mass_kg.note: EltonTraits MamFuncDat BodyMass-Value 761.9 g, which sits inside Wikipedia's 453.6-1134 g range and matches it closely at the low end; the midpoint of that range would be 794 g, close enough that the sourced value is used.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of Wikipedia's 50.8-76.2 cm total length, nose to tail tip, with a body of 25.4-38.1 cm and a similar tail length.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Derived, not quoted: the article gives the hind foot as 5.1-8.2 cm but no shoulder height. Shoulder height is taken as about four times the mid hind-foot length, the usual allometric relationship for a sciurid standing on its hind limbs, which gives 4 x 6.65 cm = 26.6 cm. A quoted measurement would replace this; the field is optional, and it is present because the validator asks for it on a quadruped.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Weakly sourced, and the only age figure the article gives: 'the reproductive longevity of the squirrel may be over 12 years'. That is a ceiling on breeding age rather than a measured wild longevity, so 12 is an upper bound taken as the best available value; the source gives no mean or maximum wild lifespan and the field is not optional.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-Seed 50, Diet-PlantO 30 and Diet-Fruit 20 give the fractions directly; Diet-Seed is mapped to the schema's mast, since for this species the seeds it caches are acorns and hickory, walnut and pecan nuts, and Diet-PlantO to browse for buds, leaves and shoots. The record also cites the fact that it takes insects, tubers, roots, bird eggs and fungi, but at a trace share too small to carry against a sourced 100 percent of the three main items.

traits.social.note: "Fox squirrels are not particularly gregarious or playful; in fact, they have been described as solitary and asocial creatures, coming together only in breeding season."

traits.activity_pattern.note: EltonTraits Activity-Diurnal 1 with Nocturnal and Crepuscular both 0, and Wikipedia's 'Fox squirrels are strictly diurnal' agree exactly.

traits.defense.note: Flees, typically up a tree, from the many predators listed for the species; judgement mapping to the schema's single-value field. When threatening another fox squirrel it stands upright with its tail over its back and flicks it, which is display rather than escape.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.3. 'Tolerant of human proximity, and even thrive[s] in crowded urban and suburban environments', nesting in attics and raiding crop food, but still gives bark and distress-scream alarm calls and bolts when approached closely.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-Value 'Ar' gives the arboreal stratum as the primary one, and the article says it spends more time on the ground than most other tree squirrels and is often seen foraging on the ground hundreds of metres from the nearest woodlot. The 0.55 ground share is judgement on that description, between the two.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: "Tree dens are preferred over leaf nests during the winter and for raising young"; when den trees are scarce, leaf nests are used year-round.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet exactly. The cavity-versus-drey nesting split of 0.7 and 0.3 follows the article's statement that dens are preferred for winter and for rearing young, with leaf nests used when dens are scarce; shrub_thicket is the summer drey and general cover, weighted by judgement.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Quoted directly in the notes field: tolerant of human proximity, thriving in crowded urban and suburban environments, and exploiting habitations for food and nest sites including attics. impervious_max, flight_distance_m and road_mortality are authored judgement and are not quantified in the source.

habitat.density_per_ha.note: Judgement: the article gives no density but describes it as common in forest patches of 40 hectares or less and in urban neighbourhoods with trees, and as absent from stands with dense undergrowth. A home range of a couple of hectares for a non-territorial animal gives typical 0.5 per hectare, and min and max are an authored tenfold band either side, following the convention used for turdus-migratorius and sciurus-carolinensis.

seasonal.strategy.note: No dormancy or migration is described; it is active year-round, storing food instead.

seasonal.phases.note: The mid-December and early-January and June estrus, two litters a year with yearling females at one, 44-45 day gestation, late-January earliest litters and mid-March and July for most births, the eye and ear opening times, weaning at 12-14 weeks, self-support at 16 weeks, September-October dispersal, first-winter dening with the mother, and autumn caching are all stated in the article.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration is authored: self-supporting at 16 weeks is 112 days, and dispersal at about six months is treated as the end of the juvenile stage's dependence rather than folded in. scale is authored judgement for a neonate squirrel against a 762 g adult.

vocalizations.note: Barking as the most common call, distress screams as the threat warning, the clucking and chucking of groups in spring and autumn, tooth chatters and breathy barks as stress signals, grunts and squeals from a restrained animal, and the mating whine all come from the article's Behavior and ecology and Vocalization passages. Months, time windows and cooldowns are authored judgement; the mating whine's months follow the two estrus periods. No open source gives frequency bands, so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Colours from the Description: in most areas the upper body is brown-grey to brown-yellow with a typically brownish-orange underside; the darker Appalachian form has white bands on the face and tail and the southern and lower-Mississippi form is uniformly black. The record renders the common brown form, which is what a Michigan garden holds, with markings available for the darker morphs. Proportions and the tail-fluff and ruff parts are authored judgement; the ruff is parented to the neck. No open source describes the eye colour, so eye is a judgement value.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program. food_tag is mast because it caches and eats shelled nuts and acorns; rest_sun_lo_deg and rest_sun_hi_deg set to -90 and -6 per the program's description for a diurnal species, which EltonTraits and Wikipedia both confirm; flee_m 12 m, calm_m 30 m and food_m 30 m are judgement scaled for a bolder and more ground-bound animal than the fox example the program defaults to, with flee_gait gallop for the short dash up a tree.
